title: Two Sides of English
blurb: Understand North American vs British English

steps.html:
An American travel editor and a British presenter spend eight minutes discussing the same three holidays. They agree about everything and they use different words for almost half of it.

  • Follow a longer interview and pick out the detail
  • Recognise North American and British words for the same thing
  • Use the past perfect inside a longer story
  • Write a recommendation for a learning holiday

steps.prompt: What does that tell you about how these differences work in practice?
options: That she is deliberately demonstrating American usage for the listener.
That the words are simply hers, and the difference is only visible to somebody listening for it.
That she has forgotten the British equivalents.
steps.answer: That the words are simply hers, and the difference is only visible to somebody listening for it.
steps.why: Nobody in the recording treats the choice as remarkable. That is what makes it a genuine sample rather than a demonstration.

steps.title: Keeping two time levels straight across several sentences
steps.html:
You met the form in Lesson 10. Here it has to hold a whole narrative together.

In a longer story, the past simple carries the line of events and the past perfect keeps stepping back off it. The reader can only follow if you are consistent about which is which.

A useful test: the past simple moves the story forward in time; the past perfect does not. If a sentence takes the reader backwards, it needs had.

Once you have established the earlier time, you can often drop back into the past simple within it: She had booked the course in March. She paid the deposit, printed the confirmation and forgot about it. The past perfect opens the flashback; the past simple runs it.

Words that signal a step backwards: by then, by the time, already, before that, earlier, until then, never … until. Words that keep you on the line: then, next, after that, an hour later, finally.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences from one continuous story. Notice which ones move forward.

I booked the falconry course in January.
Forward. Past simple.

I had never held a bird of any kind before.
Backwards. Past perfect.

By the time I arrived, the group had already started.
Both: arrival on the line, start before it.

They gave me a glove and explained the rules.
Forward, twice.

The instructor had been working with the same falcon for nine years.
Backwards, and it answers how long.

Then the bird landed on my arm.
Then keeps you on the line.

Nobody had told me how heavy it would be.
Backwards — the telling should have happened earlier.

After that we walked through the castle grounds.
Forward.

I had booked it as a joke. I paid the deposit and forgot about it.
Past perfect opens the flashback; past simple runs it.

Until that afternoon I had not understood what people saw in it.
Until + past perfect.

steps.title: Threading two time levels through four sentences
steps.html:
1. The events, in real order: (1) she read about the school in March; (2) she booked it in June; (3) she arrived in September; (4) the course had changed to a different building.
  2. Choose the line of the story. Tell it from the arrival: She arrived in September. Past simple.
  3. Everything before that goes backwards: She had read about the school in March and had booked it in June. Two past perfects, one sentence.
  4. Fact (4) is also earlier than the arrival, and it was done by somebody else: The course had been moved to a different building. Past perfect passive.
  5. Result: She arrived in September. She had read about the school in March and had booked it in June. By then the course had been moved to a different building.

steps.title: Write your recommendation.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Tell one short story from it, and use the past perfect at least twice inside that story.
steps.placeholder: If you have ever wanted to …
steps.html:
• Open by naming who the course is for.
  • Say what it is, where, and how long.
  • Tell one short story from your own experience of it.
  • Use the past perfect at least twice inside that story.
  • Close with what you take home.

Useful language

  • If you have ever wanted to … but never got the chance, this one might be for you.
  • It's kind of like …
  • The cost of the course includes …
  • By the time I arrived, I had already …
  • I had never … until that week.
  • You come home with something more useful than a souvenir.
steps.modelHtml:
Two days of bread, near Almaty

If you have ever wanted to learn to bake properly but never got round to it, this one might be for you. It is a two-day course in a village an hour outside the city, run by a woman whose family has had the same oven since 1961.

I booked it out of season, in November, which meant there were four of us instead of twelve. By the time I arrived I had already convinced myself it would be too basic. It was not. I had never used a wood oven, and I had certainly never understood how much of baking is waiting.

The cost includes lunch, which is the best meal I have eaten in years. You go home with flour in your bag and something more useful than a souvenir.
